title: Why Splitting the Bill Makes Everyone Order More
request: A game theory comedy short: splitting the bill equally makes everyone order more (the diner's dilemma). Script written by Claude, approved by Biku 2026-10-16.

lines.speaker: trainer
lines.text: Why does splitting the bill make everyone order more?

lines.speaker: copycat
lines.text: Let's just split it four ways. Easier.

lines.speaker: saint
lines.text: A small salad for me, please.

lines.speaker: copycat
lines.text: Then I'll have the lobster too.

lines.speaker: trainer
lines.text: When you split the bill, every extra dish costs you only a quarter of its price.

lines.speaker: trainer
lines.text: So everyone orders more, and everyone pays more.

lines.speaker: trainer
lines.text: Economists tested this in a real restaurant. When the bill was split, people ate more.

lines.speaker: trainer
lines.text: Even the one who only had water.

sources: Uri Gneezy, Ernan Haruvy and Hadas Yafe, "The Inefficiency of Splitting the Bill", The Economic Journal, vol. 114, no. 495, April 2004, pages 265 to 280. A field experiment in a restaurant: diners who split the bill equally ate more than diners who each paid for their own, and they said they preferred paying for their own. https://ideas.repec.org/a/ecj/econjl/v114y2004i495p265-280.html
What the story invents: the four friends, the restaurant and the prices. Three lobsters at $60 is $180, split four ways $45 each, the glass of water included.
